rows.34:9560:
...Where is that rubellite now, you ask?
I heard it was put in Okawa's grave.{p}
rows.34:95d0:
Apparently she died with the rubellite clutched tight in her hand.
So it was buried in the grave along with her.
Oh, yes. Fujiomi, you know... he's still alive.
Okazaki was hopeless too, wasn't she?
Imagine leaving alone the very first person she should have cursed.
I wonder if she was so consumed with bitterness that she could no longer tell one from the other.
...Well, never mind.
It has nothing to do with me.{p}
rows.34:974c:
By the way, this story is going in the school paper, isn't it?
I do hope nobody who reads it gets the idea of taking the rubellite that's in Okawa's grave for themselves.
Heh heh...
That's the end of my story.
...Still, the seventh one is awfully late, aren't they?{p}What will you do, {a}{f:|}?
It's about time we went home, don't you think...?{p}
rows.34:9874:
If you don't know, I'll tell you.
Okawa tried to steal the rubellite from Okazaki's grave.
I wonder what kind of nerve that girl had.
She seemed to think stealing from the dead was fine, as long as nobody found out.{p}
rows.34:9958:
Heh...
I suppose you just can't wait to hear what happened to Okawa, is that it?
Very well.
Then let's go on with the story.
For Okawa, finding out where Okazaki's grave was took no effort at all.
She only had to go to the Okazaki house and say she was a junior from Okazaki's school, that she'd happened to hear about her, and that she'd very much like to visit her grave.
Say that, and they would hardly refuse.
They'd suspect nothing, and kindly tell her where it was.
And that's exactly what she did.
Okawa waited until late at night, and then she made her move.{p}
rows.34:9b48:
I think graveyards are frightening even in broad daylight.
And this was the middle of the night.
A high school girl, all by herself.
That's not something just anyone could do, surely.
And her purpose was to rob a grave, no less.
Okawa must have had nerves of steel.
Or perhaps the rubellite sleeping in the grave was calling her to it.
Heh heh...
In any case, she moved the gravestone aside and took Okazaki's urn out from inside.{p}
rows.34:9ca4:
And when she opened the urn...
"Aaah!☆"
There was no rubellite in there at all.
All that was inside were fragments of burnt bone and ash.
"Wh-why...?"
For a moment, Okawa was at a loss.
But then she thought it over.
If the rubellite had been burned along with Okazaki's body...
then the rubellite really was in this urn after all, wasn't it?
So she took the ashes from the urn home with her.
She really had some nerve, didn't she?
That's not how a normal person thinks.
Well, I suppose it just shows how badly she wanted the rubellite.{p}
rows.34:9ecc:
Then that night, the ghost of a woman in a school uniform appeared before Okawa.
Okawa got a terrible fright and tried to run away at once.
But...
It felt as if some invisible force were holding her down.
She was in agony, and she went pounding on the walls all around her.{p}
rows.34:9fc4: Seeing the state Okawa was in, the ghost smiled with satisfaction.{p}
rows.34:a004:
And in the ghost's hand was a pendant that looked like the rubellite...
The ghost said,
"You fool, Okawa.
The rubellite was never buried with me.
But, well, never mind.
In honor of your persistence, I'll make you a present of it..."
Hearing that, Okawa drifted unsteadily toward the ghost.
Thoughtless, I suppose you'd call it.
And she reached out her hand to take the rubellite.
And then...{p}
rows.34:a1b0:
"Gyaaaah!☆"
Okawa was strangled.
By Okazaki's ghost.
With the rubellite's pendant chain...{p}
rows.34:a3b0:
They say she was found killed, her mouth stuffed full of something like ash.
No doubt that ash was...{p}
rows.34:a4a4:
You see, they say Okazaki never once used the rubellite's power.
At the prices back then, the rubellite was worth enough to buy a house.
So it was kept carefully locked away in a safe.
That's why, even though she knew what it could do, she never asked it for a single wish.
Apparently her parents meant it to be part of her trousseau when she married.
Though, of course, Okazaki died before that could happen.
In a traffic accident.
The rumors everyone spread were just the facts with a tail tacked on.
So what does that make Okawa, who let them lead her around by the nose?
They say the rubellite pendant wasn't in the room where Okawa died.
Okazaki's ghost must have taken it back home with her.
I imagine it's back in the safe at her house again by now, don't you?{p}
rows.34:a748:
...{a}{f:|}.
What is fate, I wonder...
......{p}That's the end of my story.
But the seventh one still hasn't come, have they?
What shall we do?
Well, {a}{f:|}...?{p}
rows.34:a808:
I see...
Then perhaps I'll tell you a little about Okazaki.{p}
rows.34:a86c:
Okazaki, you see, was the daughter of quite a powerful zaibatsu family.
And her father acquired the rubellite on a trip abroad.
They say it was worth enough to buy a house even at the prices back then, so as a little souvenir from abroad, it's far beyond anything people like us would call normal.
She adored that stone.
Back then, nobody paid any mind yet to the idea that it was a stone that brought happiness.
But since it was a rare stone even by world standards, it seems it became the talk of the school.
And the girls who told Okawa about her must have heard that rumor from somewhere too.
Okazaki was a true young lady of good family.
She'd never known hardship, and she'd been raised with great care, so she was gentle and honest by nature.
To put it kindly, she was pure.
To put it unkindly, she had no sense of caution, I suppose.
To anyone looking on, she was truly happy.
She grew up with all her father's love lavished on her alone, and her classmates fawned over her, too.{p}
rows.34:abcc:
But even a girl like her had one thing she could never have.
Her mother's love.
Okazaki's parents were divorced.
For as long as she could remember, she'd lived with her father.
And so she always thought to herself
that she wanted to live with her mother too.
But she had no idea at all where her mother was or what she was doing.
Because whenever she brought up her mother, her father always fell silent.
Then, one day...{p}
rows.34:ad70:
There was a day when Okazaki stayed late at school.
Back then, there was no new school building yet.
Most classes were held in the old school building.
The old school building is in a terrible state now, isn't it?
The wooden walls and floors are rotting, and cobwebs hang thick everywhere.
Of course, it was in better shape back then.
Even so, they say the building had a musty smell, and on rainy days water leaked in all over the place.{p}
rows.34:aed4:
Don't you find it strange that the daughter of a zaibatsu family went to a school like that?
The truth is, our school was her mother's alma mater.
She found that out when she was in junior high.
She came across her mother's uniform at the back of an old closet, and that's how she learned the truth.
That's why she took the entrance exam for our high school.{p}
rows.34:b14c:
She heard the sound of an organ.
{a}{f:|}, have you ever remembered the past and felt wistful?
Nostalgia, I suppose you'd call it.
That feeling that's somehow fond and somehow sad.
The organ had a tone that made you feel just like that.
She was captivated by the music at once.
And she peeked into the music room through the window.{p}
rows.34:b290:
Inside, a beautiful schoolgirl was playing the organ.
What year is she in?
Is she in the music club?
Wondering such things, Okazaki listened, entranced, to the girl's playing.
At the time, music classes used the piano, so the organ always sat gathering dust in a corner of the music room.
But that organ gave out a sound as vivid and sensuous as a living human voice, and it echoed in Okazaki's heart.
After a while, the girl noticed Okazaki watching her.{p}
rows.34:b42c: And she stopped playing the organ.{p}
rows.34:b460:
Okazaki was flustered, thinking she'd interrupted.
"I-I'm sorry.
Please, go on playing.
I'm leaving now anyway..."{p}
rows.34:b4f8:
Then the girl, her eyes lowered to the keys, said this.
"...That's not it.
It isn't that you're in the way."
"Oh... I see.
Um, the organ has a beautiful sound, doesn't it?"
"......"
The girl kept her head down and said nothing.
"Um... I'm sorry.
I guess I really am in the way..."{p}
rows.34:b6c0:
"You're not in the way at all."
The beautiful girl's voice reached her.{p}
rows.34:b710:
Okazaki doubted her ears for a moment and turned around.
Then the voice went on.
"You're not in the way at all..."
...Okazaki felt strange.
Was that really the voice of the girl from before?
Maybe she had only imagined it.
With those thoughts in her head, she ran out of the old school building.{p}
rows.34:b8e8:
She had it made into a pendant.
They say she treasured it.
And whenever she wished she could see that girl again, she would squeeze the rubellite tight.
As if she were asking the rubellite for a favor.
And then...{p}
rows.34:b9e8:
She saw her again.
That beautiful girl.{p}
rows.34:ba14:
The girl was playing the same organ music Okazaki had heard that day.
It was a strange tune.
Okazaki was enraptured.
She stood outside the music room, quietly listening to the organ.
Determined not to interrupt this time.{p}
rows.34:baf4:
After that, Okazaki often made her way to the music room to listen to the organ.
Making a wish on the rubellite each time.
Because when she did, she could always see that girl she had never been able to meet before.
Every time, Okazaki listened to her play and spent moments that felt like a dream.
Okazaki lived a life of luxury, but she had her own troubles too.
Friendships at school, her studies, the loneliness of having no mother...
At times like that, she always comforted her heart with the sound of that organ.{p}
rows.34:bcb4:
She went to listen to the organ after school, when no one was around.
When people stayed late at school, she would wait until night and sneak in to listen.{p}
rows.34:bd54:
Before long, the fact that she sometimes stayed late at school became the talk of everyone.
What on earth was she doing, they wondered.
But no matter who asked, Okazaki never told the truth.
She thought that if she told anyone about the music and everyone started going to the music room, her precious time would be lost.{p}
rows.34:be74:
One day, Okazaki came to the organ without making a wish on the rubellite.
The music room was filled with the smell of the building's wood.
The organ stood there in silence.
"I wonder what it would sound like if I played it..."
As if drawn in, she went up to the organ.{p}
rows.34:bf98:
Okazaki had never taken organ or piano lessons.
But she wanted to try playing that organ, the one with that beautiful tone.{p}So what do you think she did?
rows.34:c054: She was going to play, but stopped
rows.34:c06c:
She slowly pressed down a key.
......
But...
No sound came from the organ.
"Oh, so some of the keys don't make a sound..."
And yet that woman could play it so wonderfully.
Thinking that, Okazaki reached for another key.
......
"...?"
But again, no sound came out.
"...Oh, I forgot to pump it.
It won't make a sound unless you play while pressing the pedals with your feet."
Pumping the organ's pedals, she pressed the next key.
......
"......"
But there was no sound.
She began to feel somehow frightened, and, still pumping, she pressed key after key all over the keyboard.
"Wh...★"
But the organ still made no sound at all.{p}
rows.34:c320: ...She decided to find out who the woman playing the organ really was.{p}
rows.34:c360:
Perhaps that girl was not of this world.
She had that premonition as she went.{p}
rows.34:c458:
To the deserted music room at night.
Back then, the floor of that hallway was half-rotten in places.
When you walked on it, it creaked as if it were about to give way.
She thought to herself:
had the school at night always been this eerie?
She'd always come in high spirits, looking forward to the organ, so she'd never once thought of it as frightening.{p}
rows.34:c594:
As she drew near the music room, she heard the organ, as always.
She took a deep breath, then peeked into the music room through the window.
And then...
There was no one in the music room.
The organ was playing all by itself, its keys rising and falling on their own.
Just then, Okazaki suddenly sensed someone behind her.
She turned around fearfully, and...{p}
rows.34:c6e4:
"Ah...!"
The girl who always played the organ was reaching out to put a hand on her shoulder.{p}
rows.34:c750:
"N-noooo!☆"
Okazaki, startled, tried to shake off the girl's hand.
But Okazaki's hand passed right through the girl's body.
The girl's body was like air; there was nothing to touch.
For an instant, the girl's face twisted with sorrow.
But Okazaki couldn't think at all.
She just ran off down the hallway...{p}
rows.34:c894:
That night, Okazaki lay on her bed, thinking.
What had that girl been?
Through the rubellite's power, she'd learned the girl wasn't human, but...
Was she a ghost...?
If so, whose ghost could she be?
Okazaki's thoughts raced.
Just then...{p}
rows.34:c9a4:
She was seized by paralysis.
In the dim room lit by a small light, her arms and legs went rigid, as stiff as lead.{p}
rows.34:ca28:
"Do you want to know?"
A voice came from somewhere.
"Do you want to know who the girl playing the organ really is...?"
It sounded like a woman's voice.
A low woman's voice that seemed to rumble up from the ground.{p}
rows.34:cae0:
(Wh... who's there?)
Okazaki tried to cry out.
But all that came from her mouth was a wheezing breath.
"Yukie, my sweet child..."
The voice said that out of nowhere.
Mother?
Okazaki was bewildered.
She had half suspected it all along.
That her mother had died somewhere.
And that the girl playing the organ was...
in fact her own mother.
Sweat broke out on Okazaki's forehead.
It was a sultry night.{p}
rows.34:cc8c: She strained her eyes in the faint light, trying to find the woman the voice belonged to.{p}
rows.34:cce8:
Then suddenly the light went out.
A woman's low voice rang out, as if shaking the bed.
"Yukie.
Stop going to the music room.
Or you'll be cursed to death.
Understand? ...Listen carefully.
You told the rubellite you wanted to know who the girl playing the organ really is.
She is..."
Just then, the sound of an organ came from somewhere.
And besides the low woman's voice, she heard a beautiful woman's voice.
That voice had a clear ring to it that was somehow nostalgic.{p}
rows.34:cee0:
I'm the one who's your mother.
Let me play the organ for you.
After all, I parted from my husband when you were still just a baby.
Let me play you a lullaby.
My sweet Yukie..."
Okazaki grew sleepier and sleepier.{p}
rows.34:cfd0:
"No!☆ Yukie!
You mustn't fall asleep.
Don't let her fool you.
You'll be killed.
Yukie, trust me..."
This time, it was the woman's low voice.
The two women's voices echoed through Okazaki's head.{p}...{a}{f:|}.
Which one do you think was her real mother?
rows.34:d0d8: The clear-voiced woman who played the organ
rows.34:d100: The low-voiced woman who paralyzed Okazaki

notes: 34:a280: 'She strangled Okawa' - subject is Okazaki's ghost (named in the line before).
